text: A hunting query or an ad-hoc investigation query can return dozens of rows, and only one or two of them might actually matter. This lesson covers the bookmark, the tool that saves exactly that specific result, and how bookmarks accumulate into a real case file as an investigation progresses.

A bookmark saves the query itself, the matching row or rows, and a timestamp, as a standing record an analyst can return to later instead of relying on memory or a screenshot in a separate notes app. That matters because an investigation can stretch across hours or even span a shift change, and a bookmark is a durable, in-platform record that the specific thing it captured actually mattered.

A bookmark's real value in an active investigation comes from being pinned to an incident. Pinning attaches the saved result directly to the incident record, so it shows up alongside its alerts, entities, and investigation graph, not off in a separate list someone has to remember to check. A sign-in a hunting query surfaces, that the incident's own alerts never flagged, becomes visible to the next analyst immediately once it's pinned.

A single incident rarely gets solved from one result. As an investigation deepens, an analyst runs several queries, bookmarks the results that actually matter, and pins them all to the incident. Those pinned bookmarks accumulate into something closer to a case file, a running, timestamped record of the evidence behind the final verdict, something another analyst or an auditor can actually verify later.

This chapter's four pieces are one real investigation, viewed in sequence: an incident surfaces in the queue, triaged by severity; its graph and entity timelines scope what's connected; a hunting query proactively surfaces what alerts missed; and bookmarks capture every piece of evidence, pinned so the whole case travels together. Next up: Chapter 7, automating the response itself with Sentinel playbooks and Azure Logic Apps.
